newsitem.title: USA: Arizona governor denies trust fund allegations.
newsitem.headline: Arizona governor denies trust fund allegations.

text.p: Arizona Gov. Fife Symington, fighting a multi-count federal fraud indictment, said Thursday that he did not tell a lender he could tap into trust funds if need be to satisfy a loan requirement.
In his fifth day on the stand, Symington also denied claims that he misled lenders by submitting differing statements on the same date, ones that cast his financial picture in two different lights.
The two-term governor told the jury that prosecutors were wrong when they asserted he lied to Citicorp Real Estate Inc. by telling officials he had ready access to the trust money.

Symington, then a prominent developer, said he did pledge to maintain a $500,000 cash reserve as a requirement to obtain a $10.5 million Citicorp loan. But he said he told a top bank official the trusts were hands off.
Documents show that company officials have said they believed the trust funds could be used to satisfy the loan requirement.
The trust allegations are among the charges being leveled against the Republican governor by the federal government.
He was indicted last year on 22 counts of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury. If convicted on even a single count he would be thrown out of office and sent to prison.

Prosecutors continued Thursday to press their claims that Symington submitted "blatantly false" financial statements in an attempt to save his crumbling real estate empire in the mid-1980s to early 1990s.

The government walked Symington through a series of financial statements during Thursday's testimony. Prosecutors showed one statement that warned the numbers may not be accurate, and another sent the same day to a different bank that was missing the same warning.

Symington said the statement missing the warning was not the most recent and that he must have pulled an old one from the file. He said it did not matter because the bank had his mother's assets to secure the loan in case of non-payment.

Prosecutors have yet to cross-examine Symington on one of the more inflammory charges in the indictment -- that he used extortion to try to get six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee. The $10 million loan was used for a Hispanic-themed shopping centre in downtown Phoenix.
They also have not questioned him about a charge that Symington lied under oath during court proceedings in his bankruptcy case. He filed for Chapter 7 in September 1995.
Symington has maintained he made mistakes, but that he did not commit criminal wrongdoing. He also has tried to shift some of the blame for the errors on his accountants.
